module_title: The United Nations and Law of Treaties: Foundational Concepts
introduction: This foundational level explores the constitutional framework of global governance—the United Nations—and introduces the fundamental mechanics of International Treaties, which act as the 'contracts' of the international community.

core_concepts.title: The United Nations Charter (1945)
core_concepts.description:
The UN Charter is the foundational treaty of the United Nations. It acts as the 'Constitution' of the international community.
- Sovereign Equality (Art 2(1)): The UN is based on the sovereign equality of all its members.
- Supremacy Clause (Article 103): In the event of a conflict between the obligations of the Members under the UN Charter and their obligations under any other international agreement, their obligations under the UN Charter shall prevail. (This is highly tested).

core_concepts.title: The Six Principal Organs of the UN
core_concepts.description:
1. General Assembly (UNGA): The 'Parliament' where all 193 member states have one vote. Resolutions are generally recommendatory, not legally binding.
2. Security Council (UNSC): The 'Executive' responsible for international peace. Has 15 members (5 Permanent with Veto power: US, UK, France, Russia, China; 10 Non-Permanent). Its resolutions are legally binding.
3. Secretariat: Administers the UN, led by the Secretary-General.
4. Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC): Coordinates economic/social work.
5. International Court of Justice (ICJ): The principal judicial organ.
6. Trusteeship Council: Suspended operations in 1994.

core_concepts.title: Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (VCLT), 1969
core_concepts.description:
Known as the 'Treaty on Treaties'. It governs how treaties are made, amended, and terminated between States.
- Definition (Art 2): A treaty is an international agreement concluded between States in **written form** and governed by international law.
- Pacta Sunt Servanda (Art 26): 'Agreements must be kept'. Every treaty in force is binding upon the parties to it and must be performed by them in good faith. A State cannot invoke its internal domestic law to justify failing to perform a treaty (Art 27).

important_entities.name: Binding vs. Non-Binding Resolutions
important_entities.significance: A critical distinction in international law. Under Article 25 of the Charter, UN Members agree to accept and carry out the decisions of the Security Council. Conversely, General Assembly resolutions (with rare internal exceptions like budget approval) are merely recommendations and do not create hard international law.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: If a question asks: 'Does the VCLT 1969 apply to oral agreements between heads of state?' **NO**. While oral agreements can be legally binding under general international law, the VCLT strictly applies ONLY to treaties made in **written form**.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: F R A N C E + U U (France, Russia, America, eNgland, China + US, UK)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Use 'F-R-C-U-U' (France, Russia, China, US, UK) to instantly recall the P5 nations holding the absolute Veto power.

exam_strategy_tips: Whenever a Judiciary question asks 'Which Article establishes the supremacy of the UN Charter over all other treaties?', unconditionally select **Article 103**.
